g1.label: 1. What does the speaker ask the audience to think about at the beginning?
g1.why: The opening lines ask the audience to think of the person at the sewing machine, not the shop.

g2.correct: A documentary about a garment factory in Dhaka
accept: A documentary about a garment factory in Dhaka
g2.label: 2. What changed the speaker’s view of fashion?
g2.why: The speaker says a documentary about a garment factory in Dhaka changed how they see their wardrobe.

g3.correct: Sign a petition, ask brands who made their clothes, and try second-hand clothes
accept: Sign a petition, ask brands who made their clothes, and try second-hand clothes
g3.label: 3. What does the speaker ask the audience to do at the end?
g3.why: The final paragraph challenges listeners to sign the petition, ask brands, and try second-hand clothes.

g4.label: 4. Where does the speech say change starts?
g4.why: The closing lines say change starts in your wardrobe, not in parliament or boardrooms.

g5.label: 5. In "Who made your jeans?", which persuasive technique is used?
g5.why: The speaker does not want the audience to call out an answer; the question is there to make them think. That is a rhetorical question.

g6.correct: It is a gerund acting as the subject of the sentence
accept: It is a gerund acting as the subject of the sentence
g6.label: 6. (Review) In "Wearing a T-shirt twice is not a sacrifice", what job does "Wearing" do?
g6.why: Review from “Showing Racism the Red Card: Gerunds”: Wearing is an -ing form used as a noun — the subject of is.

g1.label: 1. "Who made your jeans?"
g1.why: A question asked for dramatic effect, with no answer expected, is a rhetorical question.

g2.label: 2. "Cheaper, faster, trendier — that is what they promise us."
g2.why: Three parallel adjectives in a row (cheaper, faster, trendier) form a rule of three.

g3.label: 3. "You have the power to change this."
g3.why: Speaking directly to the listener with you is the persuasive technique of direct address.

g4.label: 4. "Picture the hands that stitched your jacket — hands just like your mother’s."
g4.why: The image of a mother’s hands appeals to the audience’s feelings — an emotional appeal.

g5.label: 5. "According to the United Nations, the fashion industry..."
g5.why: Citing the United Nations and a statistic borrows credibility — an appeal to facts and authority.

g6.label: 6. "We are drowning in clothes we never wear."
g6.why: Drowning in clothes deliberately exaggerates to make the point — that is hyperbole.

g7.label: 7. "We will ask. We will demand. We will change."
g7.why: Starting successive sentences with the same words (We will) is repetition, also called anaphora.

g8.label: 8. "Together, we can build a fairer fashion industry."
g8.why: We and together include the audience in the cause — the inclusive we.

g1.label: 1. ___ , let me give you the facts.
g1.why: First of all introduces the first point of a structured argument.

g2.label: 2. The industry is growing fast. ___, that growth comes at a price.
g2.why: The second sentence contrasts with the first — however signals a contrast.

g3.label: 3. Most garment workers are women, and ___, few earn a living wage.
g3.why: What is worse adds a further, stronger point to the argument.

g4.label: 4. Some say cheap fashion helps poor families. ___, the workers stay poor.
g4.why: The second sentence opposes the claim in the first — however marks the opposition.

g5.label: 5. The workers pay the price. ___, the planet pays too.
g5.why: On top of that adds a further point to an argument, similar to moreover.

g6.label: 6. ___ , what can we actually do?
g6.why: So sums up the argument so far and turns to the next step or conclusion.

g7.label: 7. ___ , we can buy less, repair more and swap clothes.
g7.why: To start with introduces the first proposal in a list of suggestions.

g8.label: 8. ___ , change starts in your wardrobe.
g8.why: In conclusion signals the closing part of a speech.
